To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 1 potential power analysis.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8’ to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: software

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
apriori other 30 0.05 0.822 0.545 Cohen’s d NA
text
A sample of 30 was planned for each experiment on the basis of an inverse-variance weighted effect size of d = .545, 95% CI [.378, .712], derived from three masked priming ERP studies, which affords 82.2% power in a paired test at α = .05 two-tailed, with additional sensitivity expected from trial-level modeling with crossed random effects (see Kim et al., 2026, for the derivation).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 6 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < .05 Black marks identify cluster membership at corrected p < .05.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 2 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 10 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 19 distinct packages/libraries: brms, cmdstanr, dplyr, emmeans, ggdist, ggplot2, grDevices, grid, jsonlite, lme4, lmerTest, patchwork, png, posterior, ragg, rstan, scales, stats, utils. Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 860 columns across 42 data files.

Issues Identified

8 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 42 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 4 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. 4 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

0 of 4 scripts ran to the end: 4 stopped with an error.

Script Result What happened
CBPT_analysis.R Stopped with an error Error in file(file, “rt”) : cannot open the connection
Figures.R Stopped with an error Error in file(con, “rb”) : cannot open the connection
Behavioral_analysis.R Stopped with an error Error in file(file, “rt”, encoding = fileEncoding) : cannot open the connection
ERP_analysis.R Stopped with an error Error in file(file, “rt”, encoding = fileEncoding) : cannot open the connection

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • Figures.R reads Figure_01_design.tiff.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A script uses a location that exists only on your computer.

  • CBPT_analysis.R reads //Data/CBPT/all_clusters.csv.
  • Behavioral_analysis.R reads //Data/Behavior/behavior_trials.csv.
  • ERP_analysis.R reads //Data/ERP/erp_trials.csv.

No other computer has that folder, and the file is also not in the deposit.

  1. Add the file to the deposit.
  2. In the script, write the location from the top folder of your project, such as data/survey.csv. In R, here::here(“data”, “survey.csv”) does this for you.
  3. Remove any setwd() lines.

Other problems in the files

  • Figures.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 68 statistical tests reported in the paper, 8 were found in the output of the code. No script ran to the end, so most results were never produced.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 4 R code files.

Run order

A dependency cycle was detected among 2 files (Behavioral_analysis.R, ERP_analysis.R): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 CBPT_analysis.R — none
2 Figures.R — none

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. 5 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: n400_primary_fit.rds.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
CBPT_analysis.R errored runtime 0.6
Figures.R errored runtime 1.8
Behavioral_analysis.R errored runtime 2.4
ERP_analysis.R errored runtime 2.5

setwd() in the code

1 script calls setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set

> stamp_tiff_dpi <- function(path, dpi) {
>   raw <- readBin(path, 'raw', file.info(path)$size)
>   en <- if (rawToChar(raw[1:2]) == 'II') 'little' else 'big'
>   u <- function(at, size) readBin(raw[at + seq_len(size)], 'integer', size = size,
>                                   signed = FALSE, endian = en)
>   u4 <- function(at) sum(as.numeric(raw[at + 1:4]) * if (en == 'little') 256^(0:3) else 256^(3:0))
>   b <- function(x, size) {
>     v <- as.numeric(x); out <- raw(size)
>     for (k in seq_len(size)) { out[k] <- as.raw(v %% 256); v <- v %/% 256 }
>     if (en == 'big') rev(out) else out
>   }
>   ifd <- u4(4); n <- u(ifd, 2)
>   ent <- lapply(seq_len(n) - 1, function(i) raw[ifd + 2 + i * 12 + 1:12])
>   tags <- vapply(ent, function(e) readBin(e[1:2], 'integer', size = 2, signed = FALSE, endian = en), 0)
>   keep <- !tags %in% c(282, 283, 296)
>   ent <- ent[keep]; tags <- tags[keep]
>   start <- length(raw); if (start %% 2) { raw <- c(raw, as.raw(0)); start <- start + 1 }
>   m <- length(ent) + 3
>   rat <- start + 2 + m * 12 + 4          # rationals follow the new directory
>   add <- list(c(b(282, 2), b(5, 2), b(1, 4), b(rat, 4)),
>               c(b(283, 2), b(5, 2), b(1, 4), b(rat + 8, 4)),
>               c(b(296, 2), b(3, 2), b(1, 4), b(2, 2), raw(2)))
>   ent <- c(ent, add)[order(c(tags, 282, 283, 296))]
>   dir <- c(b(m, 2), unlist(ent), raw(4), b(dpi, 4), b(1, 4), b(dpi, 4), b(1, 4))
>   raw <- c(raw, dir); raw[5:8] <- b(start, 4)
>   writeBin(raw, path)
>   invisible(path)
> }

> save_fig <- function(plot, name, width, height, dpi = 600) {
>   outdir <- getOption('ms.fig.outdir', 'Output/Figures')
>   tw <- getOption('ms.fig.target.width', NA_real_)
>   if (!is.na(tw)) { height <- height * tw / width; width <- tw }
>   rn <- getOption('ms.fig.rename', NULL)
>   if (!is.null(rn) && name %in% names(rn)) name <- unname(rn[[name]])
>   dir.create(outdir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
>   f <- file.path(outdir, paste0(name, '.tiff'))
>   # Text sizing is the awkward part on this machine. ragg holds text at a fixed
>   # pixel size whatever res is, and its scaling argument enlarges geometry only,
>   # so no ragg setting gives correct text at 600 dpi. grDevices scales point
>   # sizes properly, but its cairo backend fails to load here and the quartz
>   # fallback ignores compression and omits the resolution tags. So the figure
>   # is written uncompressed by quartz and the dpi is then recorded in the file.
>   grDevices::tiff(f, width = width, height = height, units = 'in', res = dpi,
>                   bg = 'white', type = 'quartz')
>   print(plot); invisible(grDevices::dev.off())
>   stamp_tiff_dpi(f, dpi)
>   px <- round(c(width, height) * dpi)
>   cat(sprintf('%-28s %4.1f x %4.1f in  %d dpi  %d x %d px  %.1f MB\n',
>               basename(f), width, height, dpi, px[1], px[2],
>               file.info(f)$size / 1024^2))
>   invisible(f)
> }

> topo_row <- function(ex) {

>   iw <- ncol(img); ih <- nrow(img)
>   L <- 0.20; T <- 0.075

>                      lab = c('O−U', 'P−U', 'O−P'))
>   rows <- data.frame(y = (1 - T) - (seq_len(3) - 0.5) / 3 * (1 - T),

>     geom_text(data = cols, aes(x, 1 - T / 2, label = lab), size = 2.9,
>               colour = 'grey15') +
>     geom_text(data = rows, aes(L - 0.02, y, label = lab), size = 2.7,
>               colour = 'grey30', hjust = 1) +
>     coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE) +
>     theme_void() +
>     theme(aspect.ratio = (ih / iw) * (1 - L) / (1 - T),
>           plot.margin = margin(1, 1, 1, 1))
> }

Duplicate files across repo mirrors

4 files are byte-identical to another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component that mirrors the same materials). They were only run once, from its first occurrence, to avoid wasted duplicate execution: Behavioral_analysis.R at https://osf.io/download/6ae376c8bdaab439d2f9316b/ (same as Behavioral_analysis.R at https://osf.io/download/6ae376c8bdaab439d2f9316b/?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db); CBPT_analysis.R at https://osf.io/download/6ae376c81397734f47f930f5/ (same as CBPT_analysis.R at https://osf.io/download/6ae376c81397734f47f930f5/?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db); Figures.R at https://osf.io/download/6ae376c9f23dcc70dff7bca4/ (same as Figures.R at https://osf.io/download/6ae376c9f23dcc70dff7bca4/?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db); ERP_analysis.R at https://osf.io/download/6ae376c9fc8ff8dab42604c5/ (same as ERP_analysis.R at https://osf.io/download/6ae376c9fc8ff8dab42604c5/?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db).

Reported vs. reproduced

68 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 8 matched (8 fully, 0 partially) — 11.8% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

MATLAB code, no reproducible output

8 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. Consider depositing the results as well, so they are visible without MATLAB installed: run diary('output.txt') (or diary on) before the analysis and diary off after to save a plain-text transcript of everything printed to the Command Window, or use publish('script.m', 'pdf') (or the Live Editor’s Export/Save As) to generate a single readable document with the code, its output, and any figures together.
