More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

All gave written informed consent and were compensated financially (40,000 KRW), under a protocol approved by the Institutional Review Board of Korea University (KUIRB-2024-0321-01).

In both experiments, participants were tested individually in an electrically shielded, soundattenuated room, and all auditory stimuli were presented through stereo speakers.

Participants were instructed to ignore the prime and respond to the auditory target as quickly and accurately as possible.

Participants were assigned to the three stimulus lists in approximately equal numbers (10, 10 and 9).

Nine participants were excluded.

Every retained participant had overall accuracy of 77.5% or above.

Every retained participant had overall accuracy of 71.3% or above.

Participants were assigned to the three stimulus lists in equal numbers.

Ethics approval statement:

All gave written informed consent and were compensated financially (40,000 KRW), under a protocol approved by the Institutional Review Board of Korea University (KUIRB-2024-0321-01).

PubPeer Comments

We checked 37 references with DOIs. No references with comments in PubPeer were found.

RetractionWatch

We checked 37 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the RetractionWatch database were found.

Replication Check

We checked 37 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the FLoRA database were found.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Spoken word recognition may benefit from orthographic information even when spelling differs from surface pronunciation. Korean Hangul preserves spelling across regular phonological changes, allowing us to compare primes matching a target's written first syllable (orthographic, O), its realized first syllable (phonological, P), or neither (unrelated, U). We report two EEG experiments with independent participant groups, using primed auditory lexical decision on the same 120 disyllabic Korean targets, with within-modal auditory primes (Experiment 1) and cross-modal visual primes (Experiment 2). In both experiments, O primes shortened response latencies and improved accuracy relative to U primes, and produced greater behavioral benefits than P primes. The O-P latency advantage was larger with visual than auditory primes. Phonological latency priming was modest with auditory primes and was not established with visual primes, whereas evidence favored no between-experiment difference in orthographic latency priming. Orthographic relatedness was associated with more positive centro-parietal amplitudes in the N400 window (350-550 ms) in both experiments, without clear evidence of a between-experiment difference. Following visual primes, it also increased fronto-central positivity in the 250-350 ms window, more than following auditory primes. The predicted P200 enhancement was not reliably established. The behavioral O-P advantage was more clearly established than a corresponding N400 difference. The findings suggest that greater surface overlap need not yield greater facilitation and support a role for orthographic relations in spoken word recognition.

1. Introduction

Spoken word recognition requires listeners to relate a continuously varying acoustic signal to stored lexical knowledge. Acoustic realizations differ across talkers, speaking rates, and phonological contexts, yet recognition usually proceeds rapidly and accurately. This raises a question about the information that allows a spoken form to be recognized across such variation.

When regular phonological processes cause a word's pronunciation to differ from its spelling, does recognition benefit most from a prime matching the syllable that listeners hear, or can a prime corresponding to the written syllable be more effective? Korean provides a useful setting for this comparison. In 억류 /əŋɲu/ ('detention'), for example, the first syllable is written 억 /əkD /, whereas obligatory phonological changes produce 엉 /əŋ/ as the realized first syllable. Previous Korean research has reported an orthographic priming advantage with visual targets (Kim et al., 2026), but whether this advantage extends to spoken targets and how this effect varies across priming modalities remain to be clarified. Spoken targets provide the surface phonological form directly, making them informative about the relative effectiveness of orthographic and phonological priming. In two EEG experiments, we compared these priming relations, using auditory and visual primes followed by spoken words.

1.1. Written-language knowledge in spoken word recognition

Evidence that spelling knowledge influences spoken word recognition suggests that listening can engage information beyond the incoming acoustic form. In auditory lexical decision, words whose rimes admit more than one spelling elicit longer response latencies than words with a unique spelling, a finding known as the orthographic consistency effect (Ziegler & Ferrand, 1998). Ziegler et al. (2003) also distinguished phonological from orthographic neighborhood effects, reporting competition associated with the former and facilitation associated with the latter. These findings indicate that properties of written language can predict performance even when the task presents spoken words.

Priming studies provide complementary evidence. Taft et al. (2008) used auditory primes whose spelling and pronunciation dissociate to examine orthographic influences while holding phonological relatedness constant. Chéreau et al. (2007) found that orthographic overlap increased auditory phonological priming, including under procedures encouraging faster responses and reversing the lexical-decision response mapping. Orthographic and phonological auditory priming can also vary across languages within bilingual listeners (Türk & Domahs, 2022). Together, these studies support a contribution of spelling-related knowledge to spoken recognition. However, evidence that spelling influences performance does not by itself establish whether a relation to a word's written form can provide a greater benefit than a relation matching its surface pronunciation.

A further issue concerns the source of these effects. Under an online coactivation account, hearing a word activates its spelling through learned connections between spoken and written forms (Ziegler & Ferrand, 1998). A related prime may then facilitate target recognition through a shared orthographic representation. Visual primes can engage that representation directly, whereas auditory primes can engage it through sound-to-spelling connections. An effect in an entirely auditory task is therefore compatible with online orthographic activation, even when no written stimulus is presented (Taft et al., 2008). In a syllable-priming task, the prime's activated spelling could then provide a common point of access to a target whose pronunciation has undergone a regular sound change.

Under a phonological restructuring account, literacy changes the phonological representations subsequently used during listening (Perre et al., 2009). Repeated associations between sounds and spellings may alter the organization of those representations, allowing spelling-related effects to arise without activation of a separate orthographic representation on each trial. Harm and Seidenberg (2004) demonstrated computationally that learning to read can alter a phonological network and improve its processing of phonological input. The relevant overlap would therefore be expressed within the phonological system used for listening. Online coactivation and restructuring need not be mutually exclusive, in that literacy has been associated with both enhanced phonological responses to speech and recruitment of orthographic regions during listening (Dehaene et al., 2010).

Both accounts predict that experience with written language can influence listening, but they differ in the representation through which that experience affects recognition. For syllable priming, their shared implication is that an orthographic prime can activate useful information even when the target's pronunciation differs from its spelling. Comparing orthographic and phonological primes therefore tests how effectively the two relations support recognition. The comparison is especially informative when the spelling-to-pronunciation difference is systematic, as the phonological prime supplies the very form that the listener encounters in the target.

1.2. Syllable relations in Korean

The syllable has been investigated as a processing unit in both speech segmentation and visual word recognition (Mehler et al., 1981). Syllable-frequency effects have been reported in Spanish and German (Carreiras et al., 1993; Conrad et al., 2009; Hutzler et al., 2004). Spanish maskedpriming findings further showed that phonological syllable overlap can facilitate lexical decisions without identical spelling (Álvarez et al., 2004). These results motivate examining orthographic and phonological syllable relations separately in a language where the two systematically diverge.

Hangul, the Korean writing system, encodes morphophonemic information. Written syllable blocks provide a stable spelling unit even when their pronunciation changes in a word.

In the example introduced above, 억 retains its spelling in 억류 although its final consonant is realized as /ŋ/. This divergence results from obligatory phonological processes and occurs in ordinary careful speech; it does not depend on optional casual reduction. Such alternations are not restricted to a few exceptional words. In the stimulus set analyzed by Kim et al. (2023), firstsyllable phonological change occurred in 9.21% of noun words and 20.93% of inflected predicates.

The obligatory character of these alternations strengthens the comparison. If a sound change were optional, a prime corresponding to the spelling might also match a surface pronunciation that listeners sometimes encounter. Here, the target's first syllable changes in ordinary careful speech, so the orthographic prime differs from the target's required surface form. This permits orthographic and phonological priming to be compared for the same spoken word, without changing the target recording across prime conditions.

Previous Korean studies have reported orthographic priming across modalities. Lee et al. (2016) presented visual syllable primes before auditory targets and reported orthographic facilitation together with phonological inhibition. In the reverse direction, Tae et al. (2017) presented auditory primes before visual targets and found orthographic facilitation for both lowand high-frequency targets. These findings motivate examining how syllable relations operate when targets are spoken and whether their effects extend to a task containing only auditory stimuli.

More recently, Kim et al. (2026) used visual monosyllabic primes and visual disyllabic targets in a masked-priming lexical decision task with high-density EEG. The study compared orthographic, phonological, and unrelated primes. Relative to unrelated primes, orthographic primes shortened response latencies, enhanced the fronto-central P200, and attenuated the centro-parietal N400. Phonological primes produced longer response latencies than unrelated primes and no early electrophysiological modulation. The authors interpreted these findings as consistent with an early contribution of orthographic syllable structure and a later competitive influence of phonological overlap.

The present experiments extend this comparison to spoken targets using the same target words. This change is important as a spoken target directly presents the surface form favored by a surface-similarity account. Any advantage for the orthographic prime must therefore occur when surface information is directly available. Auditory primes test whether this relation is effective in an entirely auditory sequence, while visual primes make the written syllable directly available before the spoken target.

1.3. Electrophysiological evidence and the timing of priming

Behavioral priming establishes whether a syllable relation affects recognition performance but does not reveal when its effects emerge during target processing. Event-related potentials (ERPs) provide complementary evidence about the time course of orthographic and phonological priming effects.

The present study examined the P200, N250, and N400 windows, guided by previous syllable-priming findings and by evidence that form-related responses can differ across stimulus modalities. The early windows assess effects preceding the N400, while the later window tests whether the priming relations facilitate processing at a latency sensitive to lexical and contextual information.

The N400 is a centro-parietal negativity peaking at approximately 400 ms whose amplitude is sensitive to lexical, semantic, and contextual information (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Kutas & Hillyard, 1980). Related primes typically attenuate the N400 relative to unrelated primes, consistent with facilitated access to or processing of the target in context. N400 effects occur for both written and spoken words, although their timing and scalp distribution can differ (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011). In Chinese auditory lexical decision, orthographic overlap of the first syllable attenuated N400 amplitude (Zou et al., 2012). Together with the Korean visualtarget findings of Kim et al. (2026), this evidence motivates testing whether orthographic priming also attenuates the N400 for Korean spoken targets.

Earlier ERP responses may indicate whether the priming relations affect processing before the N400. In visual masked repetition priming, the N/P150, N250, and N400 have been associated, respectively, with visual feature processing, sublexical form processing, and form-tomeaning mapping (Grainger & Holcomb, 2009; Holcomb & Grainger, 2006). Within this framework, orthographic effects have been observed earlier than phonological effects (Grainger et al., 2006). P200 modulation has also been reported for graphical relations in Chinese character recognition and for syllable frequency in Spanish and German (Barber et al., 2004; Hutzler et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2003). These findings demonstrate sensitivity to form properties, although they do not establish a single function for all activity in these latency ranges.

Evidence from auditory tasks further motivates examining early effects while cautioning against direct transfer of visual-component interpretations. Kwon et al. (2016) reported P200 and N320 effects of orthographic syllable neighborhood size and sound-to-spelling consistency in Korean auditory lexical decision. As these manipulations differ from priming, corresponding latencies need not reflect identical processes. Modality also affects priming-related responses. Kiyonaga et al. (2007) observed N250 repetition effects with visual targets, whereas cross-modal priming of auditory targets produced N400-like effects whose timing depended on visual prime duration.

1.4. The present study

In the present study, we examined syllable priming in two EEG experiments, using auditoryauditory priming in Experiment 1 and visual-auditory priming in Experiment 2. Both experiments used the same 120 disyllabic targets as Kim et al. (2026). For each word target, we compared monosyllabic primes matching its written first syllable (orthographic, O), its realized first syllable (phonological, P), or neither (unrelated, U). For example, 억류 /əŋɲu/ was preceded by 억 /əkD / in the O condition, 엉 /əŋ/ in the P condition, and 던 /tən/ in the U condition.

The first question was whether orthographic priming facilitates spoken word recognition.

If orthographic relatedness contributes to recognition, O primes should produce shorter lexical decision latencies and higher accuracy than U primes in both experiments. An O benefit in the auditory-auditory experiment would establish that this relation is available without visual presentation of either stimulus. The visual-prime experiment examines the same relation when its written form is supplied directly, allowing its behavioral effectiveness to be evaluated across the two presentation contexts.

The second question concerned the relative effectiveness of orthographic and phonological priming. The combination of O facilitation and P inhibition reported for visual targets by Kim et al. (2026) motivates the prediction of an O advantage over P for spoken targets. In the auditory-auditory experiment, a simple surface-similarity account instead predicts at least as much benefit from P as from O. The direct O-P contrast tests these competing predictions. Comparisons with U are also necessary to establish whether an O-P difference reflects O facilitation, P inhibition, or both.

For the ERPs, extension of the Korean visual-target pattern predicts enhanced frontocentral P200 amplitude for O relative to U at 150-250 ms, with little or no P-U modulation in this early window. In the N250 window, 250-350 ms, O primes should elicit less negative amplitudes than U primes if the corresponding form relation facilitates spoken-target processing at this latency. P primes may also attenuate negativity if phonological relatedness facilitates processing in this window. These predictions remain conditional as N250 effects established with visual targets have not consistently transferred to auditory targets (Kiyonaga et al., 2007). In the N400 window, 350-550 ms, extension of the prior Korean findings predicts attenuated centro-parietal negativity for O relative to U. All three windows were measured over frontocentral and centro-parietal regions, and direct O-P contrasts assessed whether the related conditions differed in amplitude.

Finally, between-experiment comparisons assessed whether the priming pattern varied between auditory and visual prime contexts. Both accounts motivate O facilitation with auditory as well as visual primes. Auditory primes additionally provide acoustic information that can prepare processing of the target onset, so the magnitude of P priming may depend more strongly on presentation context. As prime modality and prime-target interval differ together, these comparisons concern the combined presentation contexts.

1.5. Data availability

Stimuli, data and analysis scripts for both experiments are available on the Open Science Framework (OSF) at https://osf.io/gntqw/?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db.

2. General methods

>General methods

2.1. Participants

Participants in both experiments reported normal hearing, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and no history of neurological or psychiatric disorder. All were right-handed, which was confirmed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971).

A sample of 30 was planned for each experiment on the basis of an inverse-variance weighted effect size of d = .545, 95% CI [.378, .712], derived from three masked priming ERP studies, which affords 82.2% power in a paired test at α = .05 two-tailed, with additional sensitivity expected from trial-level modeling with crossed random effects (see Kim et al., 2026, for the derivation).

Participants in Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 were distinct individuals, and none had taken part in the earlier study. All gave written informed consent and were compensated financially (40,000 KRW), under a protocol approved by the Institutional Review Board of Korea University (KUIRB-2024-0321-01).

2.2. Design and materials

Both experiments used the 120 disyllabic Korean word targets and 120 disyllabic pseudoword foils from the earlier study (Kim et al., 2026). The word targets were originally selected from the 15-million-word Korean Sejong corpus (Kang & Kim, 2009). Mean Zipf word frequency, expressed as log-transformed occurrences per billion, was 3.85 (SD = 0.50), and mean logtransformed frequency of the targets' first syllables was 3.61 (SD = 0.52). Every word target underwent a phonological change at the first syllable, allowing its written and surface first syllables to be dissociated. Pronounceable pseudowords were created by combining the first syllable of each word target with another randomly selected syllable and served as nonword foils in the lexical decision task. None were listed as words in the Standard Korean Language Dictionary.

Each word target was paired with three monosyllabic primes, one in each of the O, P, and U conditions. Three stimulus lists counterbalanced target-condition assignments in a Latin square, with 40 word targets per condition within each list. Each participant encountered each target once, and each target appeared in all three conditions across lists. Table 1 shows example targets and their prime assignments across the three stimulus lists.

The auditory stimuli were recorded by a female native speaker of Korean with a standard Seoul accent in a soundproof room, at a sampling rate of 48 kHz with 16-bit resolution. The same auditory target recordings were used in both experiments.

Mean target duration was 645.7 ms (SD = 63.0, range 475.7 to 774.4 ms) for words and 651.1 ms (SD = 61.6, range 511.5 to 764.4 ms) for pseudowords. Target recordings were rotated across conditions with the stimulus lists.

In the spoken materials, P primes shared the target's surface onset, nucleus, and coda, whereas O primes shared the onset and nucleus but differed in the coda. The acoustic characterization of the materials, including prime-target similarity and condition differences in prime duration, is reported in Tables S1-S2 of the Supplementary Material. /k̚uŋ/ Note. O = orthographic, matching the target's written first syllable; P = phonological, matching its realized first syllable; U = unrelated, matching neither. English glosses refer to targets. Each list contained the same 120 word targets (40 per condition) and 120 pseudowords. Each participant received one list and encountered each target once. The target recordings and list assignments were shared across experiments.

2.3. Apparatus and common procedure

In both experiments, participants were tested individually in an electrically shielded, soundattenuated room, and all auditory stimuli were presented through stereo speakers. Both experiments used a primed auditory lexical decision task. Each experiment began with 24 practice trials with feedback. Only participants whose practice accuracy exceeded 70% proceeded to the 240-trial main task, which included a break after trial 120.

Participants whose overall main-task accuracy across word and pseudoword trials fell below 70% were excluded, a criterion specified in advance. The procedure was identical across Lists 1 to 3. Within each experiment, targets were presented in the same pseudorandom order across participants and lists, with prime assignments counterbalanced across lists.

Each trial began with a central fixation cross (+) for 500 ms, followed by a visual mask (####) for 500 ms accompanied by a 300 ms auditory cue (beep sound). A syllable prime and an auditory target followed, with prime modality and prime-target timing differing between experiments (Figure 1). The screen remained blank and black during auditory target presentation.

Participants were instructed to ignore the prime and respond to the auditory target as quickly and accurately as possible. They pressed response-box key 5 with their right index finger for words and key 1 with their left index finger for pseudowords within a fixed 2,000 ms response period following target onset. The intertrial interval varied across 1,000, 1,100 and 1,200 ms, during which the symbol >__< cued participants to blink.

2.4. EEG acquisition and preprocessing

EEG was recorded at 1,000 Hz with a 64-channel BrainAmp system and actiCAP Ag/AgCl electrodes (Brain Products GmbH, Munich, Germany), positioned according to the international 10-20 system. Impedances were kept below 10 kΩ, with FCz as the online reference and FPz as ground.

EEG data from both experiments were processed using EEGLAB 2026.0.0 (Delorme & Makeig, 2004) with custom MATLAB scripts. Data were resampled to 500 Hz and filtered at 0.1-100 Hz using zero-phase FIR filters applied within recorded segments. Line noise at 60, 120, and 180 Hz was attenuated using the CleanLine plugin (Mullen, 2012). Noisy channels were identified on a 1 Hz high-pass copy using criteria of 5 s for flatlines, .8 for channel correlation, and 4 for line noise; burst and window rejection were disabled. The channel exclusions were transferred to the 0.1 Hz data.

Independent component analysis (ICA) used extended Infomax, trained on the 1 Hz copy after excluding gross excursions exceeding 2,000 µV in median-centered channels, detected in 2 s windows with 2 s margins. ICA weights were transferred to the 0.1 Hz data. Components were classified using the ICLabel plugin (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019) and removed when ICLabel brain probability was below .5 and either muscle probability was at least .8 or eye probability was at least .6. Excluded channels were then interpolated using spherical splines, followed by average re-referencing across all 64 channels.

ERP analyses used an additional 30 Hz low-pass filter and a 200 ms pre-prime baseline, with prime onset estimated from each trial's logged prime-target interval. The 0.1, 100, and 30 Hz FIR filters had orders of 16,500, 66, and 220, respectively, with -6 dB frequencies of 0.05, 112.5, and 33.75 Hz. Epochs crossing recording boundaries, overlapping gross excursions, or exceeding ±100 µV at any channel during the baseline or from -200 to 998 ms relative to target onset were rejected. Correct word trials were analyzed. An additional 1 Hz high-pass filter and exclusion of trials within 21 s of recording boundaries were evaluated in sensitivity analyses.

The same pre-prime baseline rule was applied in both experiments. In Experiment 1, at a primetarget interval of 500 ms with a spoken prime of up to 391 ms, an interval immediately preceding the target falls within the response evoked by the prime, so that subtracting it would remove part of the effect under study. A target-locked baseline and a more restrictive high-pass filter were evaluated in the robustness analyses reported in Tables S3-S4 of the Supplementary Material.

2.5. Statistical analysis

Mean ERP amplitudes were measured in the P200 (150 to 250 ms), N250 (250 to 350 ms) and N400 (350 to 550 ms) intervals after target onset. The fronto-central region comprised Fz, F1, F2, FC1, FC2 and Cz, and the centro-parietal region comprised CPz, CP1, CP2, P1, P2 and Pz.

Both regions were measured in every interval, yielding six region-by-interval amplitudes per trial. Each amplitude was averaged across the electrodes of its region and the samples within its interval, and was analyzed as a separate outcome.

A Bayesian mixed-effects model was fitted for each outcome in brms 2.23.0 (Bürkner, 2017) using CmdStan 2.38.0 via cmdstanr 0.9.0 (Gabry et al., 2025), jointly analyzing both experiments. Within-experiment results are condition contrasts estimated from these joint models. Random intercepts represented differences in overall response level across participants and target words. Participants and target words were treated as exchangeable samples from their respective populations, which is the assumption the crossed random effects express. Random slopes allowed condition effects to vary across participants and words, and experiment effects and their interactions with condition to vary across words. Correlations among the random effects were estimated separately within the participant and target blocks. All models used the following fixed-and random-effects structure, with DV denoting mean ERP amplitude (µV), natural-log response latency, or binary response accuracy. Separate models were fitted for each of the six ERP measures and for each behavioral outcome, respectively. The fixed-and randomeffects structures are expressed in R/brms formula syntax. S5 of the Supplementary Material. The priors and final random-effects specification were selected after initial results were available. Correlated random effects were adopted following comparisons with earlier uncorrelated models, which broadly preserved the principal contrast patterns but affected accuracy uncertainty and some Bayes factors. Each condition-coefficient prior was also fitted at half and twice its main width, while other priors were held fixed. The tables report the minimum and maximum Bayes factors across all three widths, as their dependence on prior width need not be monotonic. Values close to three were not treated as sharp evidential boundaries, and no absence claim rests on a value exceeding three only under the wider prior. Additional robustness checks using their own matching reference fits are reported in Tables S3-S4 of the Supplementary Material.

Exploratory whole-scalp cluster-based permutation tests complemented the regional models, examining all 64 channels from 0 to 800 ms after target onset. Whole-scalp ERP clusterbased permutation tests and cluster topographies were implemented with FieldTrip (Oostenveld et al., 2011), following the spatiotemporal cluster-permutation framework of Maris and Oostenveld (2007). Full results for all nine ERP comparisons, including correction across nine comparisons and permutation uncertainty, are reported in Figure 8 and Tables S7-S8 of the Supplementary Material.

3. Experiment 1

>Experiment 1

3.1. Participants

Thirty-eight native Korean speakers were tested, of whom 29 were retained (15 female, age M = 22.90 years, SD = 2.70, range 19 to 29). Edinburgh handedness scores averaged 8.48 (SD = 1.21). Participants were assigned to the three stimulus lists in approximately equal numbers (10, 10 and 9).

Nine participants were excluded. Two were excluded for overall accuracy below 70% across word and pseudoword trials, at 50.8% and 64.6%. Three were excluded for missing or incomplete EEG recordings, and three for malfunction of the response box, which stopped registering responses either after the first few trials or after the mid-session break. One participant withdrew during the session. Every retained participant had overall accuracy of 77.5% or above.

3.2. Procedure

Participants performed a within-modal primed auditory lexical decision task with auditory syllable primes (Figure 1A). Following the fixation and mask sequence described in General methods, the spoken prime was presented and the auditory target followed 500 ms after prime onset. The screen remained blank and black during auditory prime and target presentation.

On word trials, mean prime duration was 259.0 ms (SD = 75.7) in the O condition, 366.7 ms (SD = 16.4) in the P condition and 295.0 ms (SD = 66.9) in the U condition. Spoken prime durations ranged from 139.5 to 390.0 ms, so all auditory primes ended before target onset. Prime durations differed between conditions.

3.3. Results

>Results

3.3.1. Behavioral results

Mean latency for correct responses was 1,061 ms in the O condition, 1,091 ms in the P condition and 1,117 ms in the U condition, with accuracy of 90.3%, 80.3% and 79.3% respectively.

Fourteen word trials (0.40%) received no response and were counted as errors. The latency model used 2,899 correct word trials and the accuracy model all 3,480 word trials. Participantlevel latency and accuracy distributions are shown in Figure 2. O primes facilitated responses relative to U primes (Table 2), by an estimated 5.11%

3.3.2. ERP results

Of 2,899 correct word trials, 2,418 survived artifact rejection, a retention rate of 83.4%.

Retention was near-identical across conditions when expressed as a proportion of correct trials, at 82.3% for O, 84.1% for P and 84.0% for U, so that the unequal trial counts across conditions (862, 783 and 773) follow from the accuracy difference rather than from differential artifact rejection. All 29 participants contributed data. Sixteen of the 87 participant by condition cells in this experiment contained fewer than 20 trials, with a minimum of three, and the participant contributing fewest trials supplied 4, 5 and 3 observations in the three conditions. These cells are retained, and their influence is examined below.

Grand-average regional waveforms, difference waves and scalp distributions are shown in Figure 3. ERP results are reported for both regions in each of the three windows, giving six amplitude measurements. Positive differences denote more positive amplitude for the firstnamed condition in each contrast. Posterior contrast distributions are shown in Figure 4 and representative channel waveforms in Figure S1. All estimates appear in Table 3.

For the P200, mean fronto-central amplitude was -0.16 µV for O primes, -0.24 µV for P primes and 0.05 µV for U primes. The O minus U, P minus U and O minus P contrasts were In the N250 interval, the fronto-central O minus U contrast was -0.050 [-0.656, 0.551] µV, with BF01 = 9.25, and the P minus U and O minus P comparisons also favored the point null.

In the centro-parietal region, the O minus U contrast was 0.685 [0.099, 1.273] µV, with BF10 = 1.33. The remaining comparisons favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 5.64 and 6.06. Their narrow-prior values were both close to three, so the distinction between falling just above or below that threshold is not interpreted categorically. The full ranges appear in Table 3.

For the N400, mean centro-parietal amplitude was -0.62 µV for O primes, -1.26 µV for

P primes and -1.90 µV for U primes. The O minus U contrast was 1.165 [0.523, 1.805] µV, with BF10 ≈ 66.6. The P minus U comparison was inconclusive, at 0.645 [0.003, 1.292] µV and BF01 = 1.3. The O minus P contrast was 0.521 [-0.172, 1.215] µV, with BF01 = 3.83, falling to 1.8 at half the prior width and therefore providing limited grounds for an absence claim. In the frontocentral region, all three comparisons favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 6.4, 4.76 and 10.9, although support for the first two was weaker under the narrower prior.

Across the six measurements, the clearest evidence for an O minus U difference concerned the centro-parietal N400 interval. The centro-parietal point estimates increased across the P200, N250 and N400 intervals, from 0.658 through 0.685 to 1.165 µV. This ordering describes the window means rather than establishing a peak or a difference between windows.

Fronto-central comparisons favored the point null to varying degrees across the intervals and examined priors.

The magnitude of the centro-parietal N400 O minus U effect depends on measurement choices. These sensitivity comparisons used frequentist models with matching reference fits, so the estimates quantify changes within that framework. Adding a 1 Hz high-pass filter on common eligible trials reduced the estimate from 1.282 to 0.410 µV. Changing from a pre-prime to a pre-target baseline on common trials reduced it from 1.285 to 0.559 µV. The difference waveform also diverged before target onset, so ongoing prime-related activity may contribute to the later measurement. The point estimate remained positive across the examined specifications.

Timing and acoustic checks are summarized in Table S4 of the Supplementary Material, with complete outputs retained in the analysis archive.

4. Experiment 2

>Experiment 2

4.1. Participants

Thirty-three native Korean speakers were tested, of whom 27 were retained (17 female, age M = 22.41 years, SD = 2.55, range 18 to 28; Edinburgh M = 8.81, SD = 1.33, range 5 to 10). Six were excluded, three for overall accuracy below 70%, at 67.9%, 63.8% and 66.7%, and three for malfunction of the response box, which registered no responses or stopped registering them partway through the session. Every retained participant had overall accuracy of 71.3% or above.

Participants were assigned to the three stimulus lists in equal numbers.

4.2. Procedure

Participants performed a cross-modal primed auditory lexical decision task with visual syllable primes (Figure 1B). Following the common fixation and mask sequence, the visual mask was replaced by a written monosyllable, with its presentation duration set to 50 ms. The auditory target followed immediately at prime offset, while the screen became blank and black. The visual prime used the font and display settings described in 2. General methods.

4.3. Results

>Results

4.3.1. Behavioral results

Mean latency was 1,027 ms for O primes, 1,096 ms for P primes and 1,081 ms for U primes, with accuracy of 86.4%, 76.9% and 76.6%. Fifty-four word trials (1.67%) received no response.

The latency model used 2,590 correct word trials and the accuracy model all 3,240 word trials.

Participant-level latency and accuracy distributions are shown in Figure 5. O primes again facilitated responses relative to U primes (

Table 4), by an estimated 5.79% [4.39, 7.19], and improved accuracy, with an odds ratio of 2.61 [1.88, 3.72]. Both differences were strongly supported, at BF10 ≈ 1.2 × 10¹² for latency and BF10 ≈ 4.8 × 10⁵ for accuracy. P primes yielded an estimated latency change of 1.05% [-0.37, 2.49], with an interval including no effect, and an accuracy odds ratio of 1.06 [0.79, 1.43]. Both comparisons favored the point null, at BF01 = 7.16 for latency and BF01 = 9.02 for accuracy. In the direct comparison, O primes yielded responses 6.77% [5.33, 8.16] faster than P primes and greater accuracy, with an odds ratio of 2.47 [1.72, 3.61], at BF10 ≈ 1.5 × 10¹⁶ and BF10 ≈ 7,840, respectively.

The direction of the P latency estimate corresponds to the inhibition reported by Kim et al. (2026), but the present data do not establish inhibition. The latency comparison favored the point null throughout the examined prior widths, with BF01 ranging from 3.7 to 14.9.

4.3.2. ERP results

Of 2,590 correct word trials, 2,408 survived artifact rejection, a retention rate of 93.0%, appreciably higher than in Experiment 1. Retention by condition was 92.5%, 94.6% and 91.9% of correct trials for O, P and U, giving 863, 785 and 760 trials. All 27 participants contributed data, and five of the 81 participant-by-condition cells contained fewer than 20 trials.

Grand-average regional waveforms, difference waves and scalp distributions are shown in distributions are shown in Figure 7 and representative channel waveforms in Figure S2. All estimates appear in Table 5.

For the P200, mean fronto-central amplitude was 1.80 µV for O primes, 1.45 µV for P primes and 1.24 µV for U primes. The O minus U contrast was 0.504 [0.029, 1.006] µV, with inconclusive evidence at BF10 = 1.1. The P minus U and O minus P comparisons favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 7.65 and 3.77. The O estimate was numerically in the direction of the positivity reported by Kim et al. (2026). Although its credible interval excluded zero, the Bayes factor did not discriminate between the point null and the specified alternative. In the centro-parietal region, all three comparisons favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 3.18, 6.29 and 10.1, although the O minus U value fell below three under the narrower prior. In the N250 interval, the fronto-central O minus U contrast was 1.093 [0.644, 1.542] µV, with BF10 ≈ 8,980 and approximate BF10 values ranging from 5,220 to 8,980 across the examined prior widths. The P minus U and O minus P comparisons were inconclusive, with BF10 values of 1.58 and 1.33. In the centro-parietal region, the O minus U contrast was 0.537 [0.094, 0.986] µV, with BF10 = 1.82. The remaining contrasts and their prior-sensitivity ranges are reported in Table 5.

For the N400, mean centro-parietal amplitude was -0.42 µV for O primes, -0.68 µV for

P primes and -1.28 µV for U primes. The O minus U contrast was 0.783 [0.306, 1.268] µV, with BF10 ≈ 20.5. The P minus U comparison was less informative, at 0.601 [0.084, 1.114] µV and BF10 = 1.73. The O minus P contrast was 0.182 [-0.330, 0.707] µV, with BF01 = 8.35, remaining above three throughout the prior range. In the fronto-central region, the O minus U contrast was 0.995 [0.488, 1.499] µV, with BF10 ≈ 255. The P minus U and O minus P comparisons were less informative, with BF01 = 2.94 and BF10 = 1.56.

The O minus U contrast was supported in three of the six measurements, with positive fronto-central differences in the N250 and N400 intervals, together with the centro-parietal N400 difference. The window means do not establish an exact peak or a difference in effect magnitude between regions.
