5. Comparison between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2

Behavioral and ERP robustness checks are summarized in Tables S3-S4 of the Supplementary Material.

5.1. Behavioral comparison

The between-experiment latency comparison supported a difference in P-related priming, whereas O-related priming favored the point null (Table 6). The P-related contrast was -3.04% This should not be read as a demonstration that the two O effects are equivalent. A Bayes factor of this kind compares a point null against the alternative implied by a stated prior, and is not an equivalence test against a justified margin. No such margin was specified.

The direct comparison of the two related conditions differed between experiments in latency by 3.89% [1.95, 5.90], the O advantage over P being larger in Experiment 2, with BF10 ≈ 106. The corresponding accuracy ratios were 1.57 [0.94, 2.72] for the O contrast, 1.08 [0.73, 1.61] for the P contrast and 1.45 [0.85, 2.58] for O minus P. The O-related comparison was inconclusive, with BF01 = 1.37 and a prior range of 0.682 to 2.88. The P-related comparison favored the point null throughout the range, with BF01 = 7.02. The O minus P comparison favored the point null at the main width, with BF01 = 3.22, but fell to 1.69 under the narrower prior. The three direct O-P comparisons were specified after the earlier results were known. Behavioral sensitivity checks used matching unadjusted frequentist models as references for acoustic adjustment and response trimming. Adjustment for Experiment 1 prime duration, root mean square amplitude and energy onset changed the O minus P latency point estimates little, from -3.60% to -3.64% in Experiment 1 and from -6.83% to -6.82% in Experiment 2.

The between-experiment ratio changed from 1.035 to 1.034. This stability does not establish that the advantage is independent of acoustic properties.

The P-related between-experiment latency ratio was also stable under within-participant trimming at three standard deviations, at 0.967 [0.950, 0.985], compared with 0.966 [0.949, 0.985] in its unadjusted reference fit. Table S3 reports these checks alongside the omissionhandling sensitivity for accuracy.

5.2. ERP comparison

For the centro-parietal N400, the between-experiment differences were 0.382 [-0.407, 1.156] µV for the O contrast, 0.044 [-0.740, 0.825] µV for the P contrast and 0.338 [-0.497, 1.166] µV for O minus P. All favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 3.19, 4.82 and 4.92. Each fell below three under the narrower prior, so the evidence for absent betweenexperiment differences was sensitive to prior width.

For the fronto-central P200, the between-experiment estimates were -0.734 [-1.517, 0.038] µV for the O contrast, -0.375 [-1.076, 0.343] µV for the P contrast and -0.359 [-1.179, 0.439] µV for O minus P. The O estimates differed in sign between experiments, but the direct comparison was inconclusive at BF01 = 0.913, with BF01 ranging from 0.642 to 1.59. The P and O minus P comparisons favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 3.32 and 4.51, although neither remained above three under the narrower prior.

In the fronto-central N250 interval, the between-experiment O minus U contrast was -1.144 [-1.875, -0.395] µV, with BF10 ≈ 19, favoring a larger positive difference in Experiment 2.

BF10 ranged from 12.4 to 19 across prior widths; the main and wider-prior values used the normal approximation. The P minus U and O minus P comparisons were less informative. The fronto-central N400 O minus U comparison was inconclusive, at -0.732 [-1.541, 0.056] µV and BF01 = 1.02. Centro-parietal comparisons in the P200 and N250 intervals favored the point null to varying degrees, most of them sensitive to prior width. All six region-by-window comparisons and their prior-sensitivity ranges are shown in Table 7. These are separate amplitude comparisons rather than a model testing an interaction of region, window and condition.

For the O minus U comparison, evidence favoring no between-experiment difference was most consistent for latency. The fronto-central comparison in the N250 interval instead favored a difference, while the other ERP O minus U comparisons were inconclusive or sensitive to prior width. The ERP findings therefore depend on the region and interval being measured, without establishing a formal interaction between those measurement dimensions.

5.3. Sensitivity analysis

Item-level correlations between priming and relative acoustic closeness are reported in Table S6 of the Supplementary Material. No relation was established in either experiment. This descriptive analysis was specified after earlier results were known, and non-detection does not establish the absence of an acoustic contribution to priming.

5.4. Whole-scalp ERP analyses

Exploratory whole-scalp tests used 100,000 permutations and Bonferroni correction across nine ERP comparisons (Tables S7 and S8; Figure 8). The O -U comparison yielded a positive centro-parietal cluster in Experiment 1 (observed extent 370-480 ms, p = .021) and a positive fronto-central cluster extending centro-parietally in Experiment 2 (300-420 ms, p = .048). The latter estimate was close to .05, with a 95% Monte Carlo interval of [.042, .053]. The Experiment 1 -Experiment 2 O -U difference yielded a negative anterior cluster (220-420 ms, p = .024), reflecting a more positive O -U difference in Experiment 2. In Experiment 2, P -U yielded positive central and right frontotemporal (290-390 ms, p = .034) and negative posterior and left temporal (260-430 ms, p = .022) clusters. No other comparison, including any direct O -P comparison, survived correction. The reported extents describe the observed clusters and do not establish exact effect onset or offset. S7 and S8.

6. General discussion

The two experiments showed a behavioral advantage for orthographic primes. O primes facilitated spoken word recognition relative to U primes and produced greater benefits than P primes, supporting both behavioral predictions. This ordering occurred with auditory as well as visual primes. The ERP findings provided complementary temporal information. Following visual primes, orthographic relatedness was associated with an anterior difference in the N250 interval and centro-parietal N400 attenuation. Following auditory primes, the positive centroparietal difference in the N400 interval formed part of a sustained shift that began before target onset. The behavioral advantage between the two related conditions was more clearly established than a corresponding N400 difference.

6.1. Prime modality and temporal context

The modality comparison suggests that the expression of syllable priming depends on how the prime makes linguistic information available. Phonological latency priming was more favorable with auditory than visual primes in the direct between-experiment comparison. The auditory experiment showed a modest latency benefit whose evidential strength depended on prior width, whereas the visual experiment favored the point null and did not establish inhibition. The comparative finding therefore concerns a change in phonological priming across contexts.

Orthographic latency facilitation was more consistent, with evidence favoring the absence of a between-experiment difference across the examined prior widths. Thus, the orthographic benefit extended across prime modalities while the phonological benefit was more dependent on presentation context.

One interpretation is that auditory and visual primes establish different initial conditions for recognizing the spoken target. Auditory primes provide an unfolding acoustic pattern that can prepare processing of a related onset. Visual primes provide a syllable through its orthography, with phonological information becoming available through learned print-to-sound relations.

Candidate activation and competition may consequently differ at target onset even when the nominal syllable relation is held constant. The longer prime-target interval in the auditory experiment also allows more time for these processes to develop. Modality and timing jointly define the comparison in the present design. Crossing them in a further experiment would test whether the change in phonological priming is driven primarily by the form of the input, its temporal preparation, or their interaction.

6.2. Time course of orthographic and phonological influences

The early ERP findings qualify the prediction that the visual-target pattern would extend to spoken targets. The enhanced fronto-central P200 reported by Kim et al. (2026) was not reliably reproduced, with evidence favoring its absence in the auditory-auditory experiment and an inconclusive comparison in the visual-auditory experiment. The direct modality comparison was also inconclusive. The current evidence therefore places the clearer orthographic priming effects after the P200 measurement, rather than establishing the P200 as a general index of the behavioral advantage. Early sensitivity to orthographic variables in other auditory tasks (Kwon et al., 2016) suggests that its expression also depends on the manipulation and processing demands.

Following visual primes, the orthographic relation affected fronto-central amplitude in the N250 interval, and the direct comparison supported a larger positive difference than following auditory primes. This effect indicates that orthographic relatedness between the visual prime and spoken target influenced processing by this interval. A positive anterior difference was also present in the N400 interval. One interpretation is that the two measurements sample an extended response to the cross-modal relation, rather than successive, functionally distinct components. Kiyonaga et al. (2007) likewise showed that the timing of auditory priming differs from the N250 pattern established with visual targets. Here, the positive anterior difference supplies evidence about when the priming relation affected the response, while its inconclusive comparison with phonological primes leaves the selectivity of that response unresolved.

The centro-parietal N400 attenuation following visual orthographic primes is consistent with facilitated processing of a related spoken target. This result supports an extension of the later visual-target finding to a cross-modal sequence. The auditory-auditory effect warrants a different temporal interpretation, as its N400-window difference was part of a sustained shift already present before target onset. The N400 is sensitive to several sources of lexical and contextual information (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011), making it well suited to register benefits from information shared across a prime-target pair. In these materials, that information includes orthographic relatedness together with partial surface overlap. Both experiments therefore show a later relatedness difference, while the visual-auditory waveform provides the clearer evidence of target-related N400 attenuation.

The direct comparison of orthographic and phonological primes adds an important distinction. Their behavioral effects differed clearly, whereas the N400 comparison was inconclusive in the auditory experiment and favored the absence of a difference in the visual experiment. The whole-scalp effects of visual phonological primes (Figure S8B) suggest a broader ERP response to phonological primes than the regional summaries alone convey, although their polarity does not establish facilitation or inhibition. Recognition performance consequently cannot be inferred directly from the size of this N400 contrast. Both primes may make useful information available during the measured interval, while their different relations to the target affect subsequent lexical selection or the decision to respond. This interpretation accommodates a limited difference in the ERP response together with a behavioral orthographic advantage. It does not require the scalp measurements to identify separate orthographic and phonological systems, and the data do not localize the additional contribution to a particular later stage.

6.3. Theoretical implications for spoken word recognition

The orthographic advantage places a constraint on explanations based on the amount of surface overlap. In the auditory-auditory experiment, phonological primes matched the realized first syllable and were acoustically closer to the target onset in 76.7% of items. Orthographic primes nevertheless produced greater facilitation despite their coda mismatch, and this advantage changed little after adjustment for prime duration, amplitude and energy onset. A complete surface match was therefore not the most effective prime-target relation in these materials. The orthographic advantage goes beyond a simple monotonic prediction from surface similarity.

Episodic models can generate effects of abstract properties (Goldinger, 1998), so their evaluation requires specifying how the stored experience and similarity function would produce this ordering.

For an online coactivation account (Taft et al., 2008; Ziegler & Ferrand, 1998), the auditory-auditory finding is consistent with such a contribution from spelling activated during listening. Hearing an orthographic prime could activate its written form, providing overlap with the target's stored spelling when the target is recognized. Visual primes could engage that relation directly. The orthographic advantage across both modalities thus fits an account in which learned links make written-language knowledge available from spoken input. It extends the cross-modal findings of Lee et al. (2016) by showing the advantage when the entire prime-target sequence is auditory. Earlier auditory ERP findings in Korean (Kwon et al., 2016) and orthographic N400 priming in Chinese (Zou et al., 2012) provide converging evidence that orthographic relations can matter beyond visual word recognition.

On the other hand, for the phonological restructuring account (Pattamadilok et al., 2010; Perre et al., 2009), the same result concerns the organization of phonological knowledge in literate listeners. Repeated experience connecting spoken syllables with spelling may establish phonological relations that support recognition even when the current input differs from the written form. An auditory prime could then facilitate a target through this learned organization without requiring online activation of a separate orthographic representation. In this interpretation, the behavioral orthographic advantage is compatible with literacy-shaped phonology and does not imply that phonological processing contributes little to recognition.

An account based on abstract lexical phonology (Lahiri & Marslen-Wilson, 1991) offers a further explanation. In these materials, the written first syllable corresponds to the underlying phonological form altered by regular processes in speech. An O prime could therefore support recognition through access to that form, without requiring online spelling activation or literacyinduced restructuring. As spelling and underlying form coincide here, however, the present design cannot distinguish this interpretation from the orthographic explanations. The experiment also does not test the specific representational assumptions of an underspecification model.

The theoretical contribution therefore concerns the behavioral advantage of orthographic over phonological primes. Online coactivation, phonological restructuring, and underlying-form access offer different explanations of that advantage. O primes also retain surface onset and nucleus overlap, so models must explain how these shared features and the different coda relations jointly produce the observed ordering.

6.4. Measurement considerations and future directions

Baseline placement defines the scope of the auditory-auditory N400 interpretation. A pre-prime baseline preserves activity developing across the prime-target sequence, including responses to the prime that continue after target onset (Smith & Kutas, 2015). Pre-target divergence and the smaller later difference under a pre-target baseline or an additional 1 Hz high-pass filter show that the later contrast depends on how preceding activity is treated. We therefore interpret this amplitude difference as modulation of processing across the prime-target sequence, with a targetevoked contribution that is not isolated by the present analysis. The visual-auditory result was less sensitive to baseline placement. These checks establish how the measured priming effect depends on the treatment of preceding activity.

The theoretical alternatives motivate more selective manipulations of learning and representation. Varying learned spellings while holding spoken forms and auditory exposure constant would test whether orthographic learning changes auditory priming. Selective interference with orthographic processing during the test could then examine whether the transferred effect depends on concurrent spelling activation, whereas its persistence when such activation is disrupted would be more compatible with restructuring. Literacy comparisons or novel-word learning could help separate orthographic experience from access to underlying forms. Primes equating onset and nucleus overlap while varying the coda relation would also sharpen the interpretation of O priming.

Further work should examine the orthographic advantage and the anterior ERP response with samples planned for those comparisons. The current samples and artifact-free trial counts limited the precision of several ERP estimates, and evidence for absent effects should be considered with the reported prior-sensitivity analyses. Objective prime-identification measures would also establish the role of awareness, which was not assessed here. The brief visual prime was followed directly by an auditory target without a separate backward mask, so brief exposure alone does not establish unconscious processing. These additions would clarify the conditions under which the observed advantage generalizes.

6.5. Conclusions

Korean spoken word recognition benefited more from orthographic than phonological primes.

This behavioral advantage occurred with both auditory and visual primes, while phonological priming and the anterior ERP response varied with presentation context. The findings demonstrate facilitation from O primes during listening and show that greater surface overlap need not yield greater facilitation. The ERP results distinguish the time course of relatedness effects from the eventual advantage in lexical decisions.

Stimulus presentation was controlled by E-Prime 3.0, and responses were collected using a Serial Response Box (both Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA). Visual text was displayed in white Malgun Gothic on a black background, with the font size set to 40. The 24-inch LG monitor operated at 1920 × 1080 pixels and 60 Hz.

The single bar allows correlations among the random effects within each grouping factor. Experiment 2 and U were the reference levels, with sum-coded list contrasts. PositionC was chronological trial position centered at 120.5 and divided by 100. The same random-effects structure was used for all outcomes. Posterior summaries of the group-level standard deviations and correlations for the eight main fits are reported in Table

Latency on correct word trials and ERP amplitudes in microvolts used Student-t likelihoods. Accuracy used a Bernoulli likelihood with a logit link, with omissions counted as errors. For the Student-t models, experiment-specific residual scales were specified using the distributional formula sigma ~ 0 + Experiment. Likelihood selection was informed by posterior predictive checks of preliminary models. Gaussian residuals did not adequately reproduce the observed spread and tails. Student-t residuals improved these features, although some discrepancies in latency skewness and the upper tail remained. A skew-normal latency model was also examined during this preliminary assessment. These likelihood checks preceded adoption of the correlated random-effects specification.Condition coefficients and their experiment interactions received Normal(0, 0.15) priors on the log latency scale, Normal(0, 1.5) priors on the log odds scale and Normal(0, 2 µV) priors for ERP amplitudes. Each width was set at about four times a large plausible effect in the endpoint's own units, so that the prior remained diffuse over the effects the design could detect while placing little mass on implausibly large values. Other population-level coefficients received normal priors 2.5 times as wide. Correlation matrices received LKJ(2) priors. Intercepts, group-level standard deviations and residual-scale coefficients used the weakly informative brms defaults, and Student-t degrees of freedom received a Gamma(2, 0.1) prior with shape and rate parameterization. Four chains were run with 1,000 warmup and 3,000 retained iterations per chain. No thinning was applied, the target acceptance rate was set to .99 with a maximum treedepth of 12, and the random seed of every fit is recorded in the analysis archive. Across the eight main fits and sixteen prior-width fits, all estimated parameters had R-hat below 1.006, bulk effective sample size of at least 1,179 and tail effective sample size of at least 1,188. There were no divergent transitions or maximum-treedepth hits, and the minimum E-BFMI was 0.724. Nine within-experiment and between-experiment contrasts were computed from every posterior draw and summarized by posterior means and equal-tailed 95% credible intervals.Equal-tailed intervals were preferred to highest-density intervals as their endpoints are preserved under the back-transformations applied to latency and accuracy, whereas highest-density intervals are not. Latency and accuracy estimates back-transform the posterior means and interval endpoints from the log and log-odds scales, respectively. For each contrast, BF01 was obtained as a Savage-Dickey density ratio, with the posterior density at zero divided by its analytic prior density at zero; BF10 is its reciprocal. BF10 above one favors a difference and BF01 above one favors the point null. The posterior density was estimated by Gaussian kernel density or, when zero lay more than three posterior standard deviations from the mean, by a normal approximation. The latter was used for 47 of the 216 main and prior-width estimates and is identified by an approximation sign in the text and figures. Its extreme values describe approximate orders of evidence rather than precisely established magnitudes.

84, 6.36], and improved accuracy, with an odds ratio of 4.09[2.67, 6.80]. Both differences were strongly supported, with BF10 ≈ 4.3 × 10¹¹ for latency and BF10 ≈ 5.8 × 10⁶ for accuracy. P primes produced a smaller latency benefit of 2.03% [0.78, 3.27], with BF10 ≈ 4.56; its evidential strength varied across prior widths, from 2.27 to 9.95. Their accuracy comparison favored the point null, with an odds ratio of 1.14 [0.84, 1.59] and BF01 = 9.57. In the direct comparison, O primes yielded responses 3.15% [1.78, 4.46] faster than P primes and greater accuracy, with an odds ratio of 3.59 [2.24, 6.14], at BF10 ≈ 650 and BF10 ≈ 2.0 × 10⁴, respectively. These direct comparisons were specified after the earlier results were known.The pattern was asymmetric. Orthographic primes benefited both measures, whereas phonological primes produced a smaller latency benefit. The phonological accuracy comparison favored the point null throughout the examined prior range.
